title: How Many Eggs Should You Freeze? Real Numbers by Age
tags: how many eggs should I freeze
how many eggs for one baby
description:
How many eggs should you freeze? Dr Senai Aksoy, Associate Professor of Reproductive Medicine, walks through what the studies actually show: how your age at freezing and the total number of mature eggs shape your chance of having a baby later, why twice the eggs isn't twice the chance, and how the same logic works in IVF.

In short: your age at freezing sets the odds for each egg, and the total number of mature eggs decides how many tries you get at those odds. Freezing can improve your odds later, mostly when eggs are frozen younger, but it is not a guarantee of a baby.

📖 Full article with all sources: https://draksoyivf.com/blog/how-many-eggs-to-freeze-for-baby-success/

CHAPTERS
00:00 How many eggs should I freeze?
01:07 Eggs, embryos and babies are not the same
02:05 The egg "talent show": from thaw to a normal embryo
03:14 How many eggs do you need at your age?
04:49 Does doubling your eggs double your chance?
05:56 IVF: same logic, different timing
06:47 Stimulation safety: a sensible number
07:12 Before you decide
07:59 My clinical view
08:32 Back to the dinner party
09:05 3 questions to ask your doctor

KEY NUMBERS
• Women who later used eggs frozen at 35 or younger: about 5 out of 10 had a baby. Frozen at 40 or older: about 2 out of 10 (2024 review).
• At one New York university clinic, with 20 or more mature eggs thawed: about 7–8 out of 10 women under 38, about 5 out of 10 at 38–40, and about 3–4 out of 10 at 41 or older had a baby or an ongoing pregnancy.
These are group averages from the studies below, not a personal forecast.

QUESTIONS TO ASK YOUR DOCTOR
1. How many mature eggs would you expect me to get per cycle, at my age and with my test results?
2. What's your lab's survival rate after thawing, and how many women my age have had a baby from their frozen eggs here?
3. If one cycle gives fewer eggs than we hoped, what would a second cycle realistically add?

SOURCES
• Hirsch et al., Human Reproduction Update 2024: live birth in women who returned to use eggs frozen for planned (elective) egg freezing, 10 studies, 1,517 women: https://doi.org/10.1093/humupd/dmae009
• Klein et al., Fertility and Sterility 2025: thawed mature eggs to chromosomally normal embryos, and how many women came back: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2025.12.003
• Cascante et al., Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics 2024: age, mature eggs thawed and number of freezing cycles (NYU, 731 women): https://doi.org/10.1007/s10815-024-03175-w
• Sunkara et al., Human Reproduction 2011: eggs collected and predicted live birth after a fresh IVF cycle (UK, 400,135 cycles): https://doi.org/10.1093/humrep/der106
• Polyzos et al., Fertility and Sterility 2018: cumulative live birth (fresh and frozen embryos) by number of eggs: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2018.04.039
• Steward et al., Fertility and Sterility 2014: number of eggs and the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2013.12.026
• ASRM Practice Committee 2021: outcomes after egg freezing, including outcomes of babies at birth: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2021.02.024

title: 20 Eggs = 20 Chances? Not Quite.
description:
If you freeze 20 eggs, you don't get 20 chances at a baby. Think of it as a talent show: the thaw, fertilization, growing to a day-5 embryo, and a chromosome round that gets tougher with age. At one large egg-freezing clinic, about 2–3 out of 10 thawed eggs from women who froze before 38 became a chromosomally normal embryo; at 38 or later, less than 1 out of 10.

title: “Clinically Studied”… But Did They Count Babies?
description:
Every supplement bottle sounds sure of itself: “supports egg quality,” “clinically studied.” But a supplement can give you one more egg, or a nicer-looking embryo, without giving you more babies. title: Twice the Eggs ≠ Twice the Chance
description:
More eggs help, but doubling your eggs doesn't double your chance. In one clinic's model, at 34, going from 10 to 20 mature eggs took the chance of a baby from about 5 out of 10 to nearly 7. And extra freezing cycles helped only because they added eggs: what counts is the total number of mature eggs.

title: IVF Supplements: What Really Helps? CoQ10, DHEA, Vitamin D & More
description:
Which supplements actually help with IVF? Dr Senai Aksoy, Associate Professor of Reproductive Medicine, checks the usual bottles (folic acid, vitamin D, CoQ10, myo-inositol, melatonin, antioxidants, NMN and DHEA) against one question: did the studies count babies?

In short: no supplement has been shown to give women more babies with IVF. Folic acid is for almost everyone, to protect the baby. Vitamin D, if your level is low. CoQ10 is a "maybe" for low ovarian reserve. DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live births.

📖 Full article with all sources: https://draksoyivf.com/blog/coq10-melatonin-nac-oocyte-quality-ivf/

CHAPTERS
00:00 Which supplements actually help with IVF?
00:59 How do we know a supplement works?
01:55 The Evidence Score (0 to 4)
02:53 Folic acid
03:41 Vitamin D
04:46 CoQ10: the one "maybe"
06:14 Myo-inositol
06:59 Melatonin
07:36 Antioxidant blends and NAC
08:17 NMN
08:40 DHEA
09:40 Before you add another bottle
10:40 My take
11:04 Recap and 3 questions for your doctor

EVIDENCE SCORE (Dr Aksoy's teaching scale, not an official score: how close has the evidence come to more babies?)
4 · good trials, more babies: none
3 · better eggs, embryos or pregnancy rates, not more babies: CoQ10 (low reserve)
2 · small or low-quality, uncertain: vitamin D (for IVF results), myo-inositol, melatonin, antioxidant blends/NAC
1 · lab or animal only: NMN
0 · tested in randomized trials, probably no difference in births: DHEA
Not scored: folic acid (different job: protecting the baby)

QUESTIONS TO ASK YOUR DOCTOR
1. Based on my tests, does any supplement make sense for me, and why?
2. Is anything I'm taking now unnecessary, or could it interfere with my treatment?
3. Should my vitamin D level be checked?

title: Weight-Loss Injections and Pregnancy: Do They Really Help You Get Pregnant?
description:
"One shot, zero appetite…" then "surprise, I got pregnant": on social media, the link between weight-loss injections and pregnancy looks obvious. Dr Senai Aksoy, Associate Professor of Reproductive Medicine, looks at what the studies actually show about GLP-1 medications (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide) and fertility.

In short: these medications may contribute indirectly to pregnancy chances in some women, particularly with PCOS. They are not direct infertility treatments, and they are not used during pregnancy. We also cover how long to stop them before a planned pregnancy, contraception, egg retrieval and anesthesia, and what is known in men.

title: DHEA for IVF: What 28 Trials Found
description:
A large Cochrane review pooled 28 randomized trials of DHEA and testosterone, mostly in women who respond poorly to stimulation. The answer, with moderate certainty: DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live births. DHEA isn't a vitamin; it's a hormone, with hormone side effects like acne, and the 2025 ESHRE guideline doesn't recommend it before or during stimulation. Evidence Score 0 (tested, probably no difference) on Dr Aksoy's teaching scale, not an official score.

title: Abnormal Semen Analysis: Does It Mean You're Infertile?
description:
Your semen analysis came back with asterisks, arrows and a twenty-eight-letter word? Before you conclude you're infertile, let's look at what the "normal ranges" really mean. Dr Senai Aksoy, Associate Professor of Reproductive Medicine, explains where the WHO (2021) reference values come from, why a number below the limit is not a verdict, why the test is repeated, ideally three months later, and when to see a urologist or an andrologist.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Abnormal semen analysis = infertile?
00:50 The lab report that scares you
02:16 What the WHO says
02:39 Oligo, astheno, terato: the translation
03:24 Where do the normal ranges come from?
04:25 Morphology: 4 out of 100
05:23 What the studies show
05:52 Why repeat the test three months later?
07:06 Testosterone: a bad idea
07:48 When to see a urologist or an andrologist
09:07 Emergencies that can't wait
09:26 My view as a physician
10:00 Three questions for your doctor

THE NUMBERS MENTIONED IN THE VIDEO
WHO 2021 lower reference limits: the 5th centile of men whose partners got pregnant within a year. They are not a fertility cut-off, and some labs use other ranges, so always check the range printed on your own report.
• Semen volume: 1.4 mL
• Sperm concentration: 16 million/mL
• Total sperm number: 39 million per ejaculate
• Total motility: 42%
• Progressive motility: 30%
• Vitality: 54%
• Normal forms (morphology): 4%

The roadmap (UK NICE guideline, 2026)
• Two abnormal semen analyses: physical examination; hormone blood tests to be considered
• Concentration persistently below 5 million/mL: chromosome analysis (karyotype) to be considered
• No sperm at all, with no known cause: karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion test
• Below 1 million/mL, with no known cause: Y-chromosome microdeletion test
• Suspected blockage or absent vas deferens: CFTR (cystic fibrosis) gene test

THE THREE QUESTIONS TO ASK YOUR DOCTOR
1. Has the result been confirmed by a second test?
2. Do we need a physical exam and a hormone blood test?
3. Should we consult a urologist or an andrologist?

Sudden, severe pain in a testicle is an emergency: go to the emergency department or call 911 (US), 999 (UK), 112 (EU) or your local emergency number. A lump in a testicle: see a doctor promptly.

REFERENCES
[1] WHO. Laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, 6th edition, 2021
[2] Campbell MJ, et al. Andrology. 2021;9(3):817-22. Distribution of semen examination results, 2020. PMID 33528873

[4] Hotaling JM, et al. Fertil Steril. 2011;95(3):1141-5. Isolated teratozoospermia and IVF/ICSI outcomes, meta-analysis of 4 studies. PMID 21030014

title: When Do You See the Heartbeat After IVF? First Ultrasound Explained
tags: when do you see heartbeat IVF
description:
When can you see the heartbeat at the first ultrasound after IVF, and what if there's no cardiac activity yet? Dr Senai Aksoy, Associate Professor of Reproductive Medicine, explains what the doctor looks for, week by week.

In short: cardiac activity is usually visible at around 6 weeks of pregnancy. Too early is not necessarily a bad sign: a follow-up scan at least a week later is often planned before drawing any conclusion.

Inside: how weeks of pregnancy are counted after an embryo transfer, what a transvaginal scan shows and when, the criteria for a follow-up scan, what the studies say about pregnancies that continue, ectopic pregnancy, and the warning signs that should never wait for your next appointment.
